qs.q: A patient with dermatophytosis presents with tinea pedis. The organism is identified by which morphological feature?
o: Yeast cells possessing thick, double-contoured walls
Broad, non-septate hyphae with right-angle branching
qs.e: Dermatophytes appear as septate hyphae with characteristic conidiophores.
qs.s: Weekly Year 3: Medical Mycology Exam - November 13, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A patient is diagnosed with tinea capitis resulting in a severely inflamed, boggy, pus-filled scalp mass known as a kerion. What pathological host mechanism is primarily responsible for this severe inflammatory reaction?
qs.e: A kerion represents an intense cell-mediated, delayed-type hypersensitivity immune response directed against dermatophyte antigens in the hair follicle.
qs.s: Weekly Year 3: Medical Mycology Exam - November 6, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A patient is diagnosed with tinea capitis caused by Microsporum canis. When examined under a Wood's lamp in a dark room, the infected hair shafts exhibit a bright green fluorescence. What biochemical substance causes this phenomenon?
o: Ergosterol breakdown in the cell wall
qs.e: Certain dermatophytes like Microsporum produce fluorescent pteridine pigments within infected hair shafts under ultraviolet light.
qs.s: Weekly Year 3: Medical Mycology Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A patient with tinea versicolor has lesions that fail to tan when exposed to sunlight. What mechanism explains this localized hypopigmentation?
o: Fungal dicarboxylic acids inhibit human tyrosinase enzyme activity
The organism actively destroys melanocytes within the basal layer
Thick scales mechanically block ultraviolet light penetration
Fungal toxins induce local apoptosis of epidermal keratinocytes
Inflammatory cytokines downregulate melanin transfer to cells
qs.e: Malassezia species produce dicarboxylic acids (such as azelaic acid) that competitively inhibit tyrosinase, preventing melanin production.
qs.s: Weekly Year 3: Medical Mycology Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A patient presents with a boggy, inflamed scalp lesion after a tinea capitis infection. Which immune response is primarily responsible for the lesion’s appearance?
qs.e: The lesion is a kerion, a Type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction to the dermatophyte.
qs.s: Mycoses: Fungal Pathogenesis, Virulence & Host Immune Defense: MCQs

qs.q: Which of the following statements regarding Tinea nigra is NOT correct?
o: Causes hyperpigmented macules on palms and soles
Is a systemic infection requiring IV therapy
qs.e: Tinea nigra is a superficial fungal infection characterized by hyperpigmented macules on the palms and soles, caused by Hortaea werneckii. It is treated with topical antifungal agents, not intravenous therapy.
qs.s: Weekly Year 3: Medical Mycology Exam - October 9, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: Which of the following is a common cause of superficial skin infection characterized by hypopigmented or hyperpigmented patches, often referred to as 'sun spots' or 'tinea versicolor'?
qs.e: Malassezia globosa (and other Malassezia species) are the causative agents of pityriasis (tinea) versicolor, a superficial mycosis characterized by discolored skin patches, particularly on the trunk and shoulders.

ai.title: Tinea (Dermatophyte Infections)
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Tinea are superficial dermatophyte infections of skin, hair or nails. They are common in low‑resource tropical settings and present as ring‑shaped lesions or scaling patches. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by microscopy or culture when available, and treatment is topical antifungals, with oral agents for extensive disease.

sections.p: Tinea refers to infections caused by keratin‑degrading fungi (dermatophytes) that invade the stratum corneum, hair shafts or nails. They thrive in warm, humid environments and spread by direct contact or fomites.
b: Common in children and adults in East Africa due to barefoot walking and communal bathing.
Lesions are usually pruritic, well‑demarcated, and may have central clearing.

sections.p: Dermatophytes are filamentous fungi (Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton) that produce keratinases to digest keratin.
b: Grow best at 25‑30 °C; do not invade deeper tissues.
Species distribution varies: T. rubrum (adults), T. violaceum (tinea capitis in Africa).

sections.p: Spores are shed from infected skin, hair or nails and survive on moist surfaces. Infection occurs when spores contact broken skin or hair.
b: Person‑to‑person contact, shared towels, clothing, bedding.
Animal reservoirs (e.g., T. mentagrophytes from pets).

sections.p: Clinical patterns are named by site: tinea corporis (body), tinea cruris (groin), tinea pedis (feet), tinea capitis (scalp), tinea unguium (nails), tinea versicolor (Malassezia, not a true dermatophyte).
b: Tinea corporis: annular erythematous plaque with raised border, central clearing.
Tinea capitis: scaly patches, hair loss, “black dot” or kerion formation.
Tinea pedis: interdigital maceration, vesicles, macerated toe webs.

sections.p: Primarily clinical; confirm with microscopy (KOH) or culture when available. In low‑resource settings, KOH prep is the most feasible.

t.b: Confirms presence of hyaline septate hyphae → fungal infection; if unavailable, rely on characteristic morphology.
Fluorescent green‑yellow hair indicates infection; not useful for Trichophyton.
Identifies species for refractory cases; often unavailable in low‑resource labs.

sections.p: Topical antifungals are first‑line; oral therapy reserved for extensive, scalp or nail disease, or when topical fails.
b: Topicals: azoles (clotrimazole, miconazole) or allylamine (terbinafine) applied twice daily for 2‑4 weeks.
Oral: griseofulvin for tinea capitis; terbinafine or itraconazole for extensive body or nail disease.
Avoid systemic azoles in severe liver disease or when interacting with antiretrovirals.

t.b: Treat empirically based on lesion pattern; reassess if no improvement in 2 weeks.
Emphasise drying skin, wearing breathable footwear, avoiding sharing towels to prevent recurrence.

sections.p: Focus on pattern recognition, risk factors, and appropriate use of limited diagnostics.
b: Ring‑shaped lesion with active border → tinea corporis.
Interdigital maceration in a farmer → tinea pedis; consider secondary bacterial cellulitis.
Scalp scaling with hair loss in a child → tinea capitis; treat with oral griseofulvin.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly spreading erythema, fever, or systemic signs suggesting secondary bacterial cellulitis.
Extensive nail involvement causing pain or functional loss.
Kerion formation (boggy, painful scalp mass) requiring systemic therapy.

faq.q: Can tinea be confused with psoriasis?
faq.a: Yes; psoriasis lacks the active, raised border and central clearing typical of tinea; KOH can differentiate.

faq.q: Why is oral griseofulvin preferred for tinea capitis?
faq.a: It concentrates in keratin and is fungistatic against dermatophytes invading hair shafts.

faq.q: What preventive measures reduce tinea in villages?
faq.a: Regular foot washing, drying between toes, wearing shoes, and not sharing personal items.

exam: A 10‑year‑old presents with patchy scalp hair loss and black dots – what is the most appropriate next step? — Perform KOH of hair pluck; start oral griseofulvin if positive.
A farmer has an annular, itchy lesion on the forearm with central clearing – which feature distinguishes tinea corporis from eczema? — Presence of an active, raised border with peripheral scaling.

A patient with HIV develops extensive tinea corporis unresponsive to topical therapy – what systemic agent is preferred and why? — Oral terbinafine; it is fungicidal, has fewer drug‑drug interactions than azoles.
You suspect tinea pedis but have no KOH slides – how do you manage? — Treat empirically with topical azole for 2‑4 weeks; advise hygiene and monitor for secondary infection.

A child presents with a boggy scalp swelling (kerion) – what is the immediate management? — Start oral griseofulvin and consider adjunctive steroids; refer for possible surgical drainage if abscess forms.

In a low‑resource clinic, how would you differentiate tinea versicolor from tinea corporis? — Look for fine, hypo‑ or hyper‑pigmented macules without a raised border; Wood’s lamp shows yellow‑gold fluorescence for Malassezia.
A patient on antiretroviral therapy develops tinea unguium – which antifungal should be avoided and why? — Systemic azoles (e.g., fluconazole) due to CYP450 interactions increasing ART levels.
What are the red‑flag signs that a simple tinea infection may need urgent referral? — Fever, rapidly expanding erythema, cellulitis, or systemic toxicity.
